newsitem.title: GERMANY: Nestle moves to thwart extortion attempt.
newsitem.headline: Nestle moves to thwart extortion attempt.

text.p: Swiss foods giant Nestle hit back on Thursday at extortionists threatening to contaminate its products unless they are paid a reported $15 million in diamonds.
Thomy, a German arm of the world's biggest food company, said it would fit protective seals on its tubes and warned consumers to stay on the alert.

Investigators have found no signs of contamination in Thomy products since a letter sent to the company earlier this week claimed to have poisoned Nestle or Thomy-branded products in 55 stores around Germany.

Police believe the letter, the third attempt to extort money from the firm in the last 12 months, may be part of a continuing campaign against Thomy and that the latest scare is merely a means of applying psychological pressure.
The threat, which was made public on Tuesday evening, sparked a nationwide alert. More than 15,000 people flooded police with phone calls on an emergency number.
Authorities have appealed to members of the public to return mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise, coffee, cocoa, tea and chocolate bought since August 1 bearing the Thomy or Nestle brand names.
Police believe that cyanide was introduced into a Thomy mustard tube in April through injections directly underneath the screw-top of the tube.
But while protective seals are designed to show up any attempt to penetrate them, the food industry accepts they are not a guarantee against poison attempts.

"It is an incredibly difficult problem...To an extent, it's up to consumers themselves to keep their eyes open for anything unusual," said Matthias Horst, business manager of the Bonn-based German Food Industry Federation.
Aside from the possible link to the two previous extortion attempts, detectives have as yet failed to turn up any significant clues in tracking down the criminal or criminals behind the letter.
Police have declined to say how much money was being demanded but ZDF television, citing anonymous sources, has quoted a figure of $15 million in uncut diamonds.
Police said they had carried out checks on stores in 12 of the 14 towns mentioned in the extortion letter and that the search for poisoned food products was largely complete.

The German Confederation of Retailers (HDE) says food retailers have to deal with two or three extortion attempts every week but that no one in Germany had so far been harmed by deliberately contaminated food.
